messages.content: I want to build an incremental Java taint analyzer that preserves interprocedural soundness when method-body edits change heap aliasing and virtual dispatch.

The goal is to update taint findings after an edit without losing flows that cross method boundaries. Heap aliasing and virtual dispatch matter because an edit can change which references reach the same object or which implementation a virtual call can invoke. Either change can affect taint behavior outside the edited method, so the incremental result has to account for those wider effects.
What is the correctness target? Is it enough for the incremental analyzer to find the important flows?

The stated target is more precise: for Java without reflection or native calls, its findings must equal those from sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation. That requires matching the reference findings, not merely finding some important flows or avoiding missed findings while adding others. The requirement does not specify how findings are represented or which context-sensitive analysis strategy to use.
So the comparison is against recomputing the analysis for the whole program after the edit?

Yes. The whole-program recomputation supplies the correctness comparison for the edited program. Incrementality changes how the result is obtained, but the required findings remain the same as those of the sound, context-sensitive recomputation within the stated Java scope.
Why call out interprocedural soundness rather than just soundness inside the edited method?

Because a taint flow can pass through calls and returns. A method-body edit can change information relevant to a caller or a callee, and the effect may continue through further calls. Looking only at the edited method would not, by itself, establish that the resulting program-wide findings match whole-program recomputation.
Can you explain the heap-aliasing concern without assuming a particular implementation?

As a general illustration, two references may point to the same heap object. If an edit changes whether that can happen, a taint written through one reference may become observable through the other, or cease to be observable that way. The references may be used in different methods, which is why a change in aliasing can have interprocedural consequences. That illustration describes the concern, not a particular test case or a chosen analysis technique.
And how does virtual dispatch fit into the same goal?

A virtual call can invoke different implementations depending on its receiver. If an edit changes which receiver objects can reach that call, it can change which implementations are possible and, consequently, which taint flows must be considered across the call. The incremental analyzer must still produce the findings of the context-sensitive whole-program recomputation when that happens.
Does the requirement say whether aliasing and dispatch have to change in the same edit?

It does not impose that interpretation. The goal explicitly covers edits that change heap aliasing and virtual dispatch; the important point is that neither kind of change may cause interprocedural effects to be lost. It also does not exempt an edit because both concerns arise together.
What does context-sensitive mean for this comparison?

It means the whole-program reference accounts for calling context rather than treating every invocation of a method as necessarily identical for analysis purposes. The requirement is to equal that reference’s findings. It does not prescribe a particular form or degree of context sensitivity for the incremental implementation.
Is reflection included if the rest of the program is ordinary Java?

The stated correctness scope is Java without reflection or native calls. No matching-findings guarantee for programs using reflection or native calls is specified here; the condition should not be silently broadened.
There is also a speed target. How should I state it alongside correctness?

Achieve at least a 3× median speedup over full recomputation on a fixed suite of 100 method-body edits. That is a performance requirement in addition to the equality-of-findings requirement, not an alternative to it.
Does a 3× median speedup mean every one of the 100 edits must run at least three times faster?

No. The specified threshold is for the median speedup over that fixed suite of 100 method-body edits; it does not say that each edit individually must reach 3×. It also does not provide timing results or a detailed measurement procedure beyond that comparison.
Could an approach satisfy the speed target by accepting a small difference in findings?

Not under these requirements. For the stated Java scope, findings must equal sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation. The at-least-3× median speedup is a separate target to meet while preserving that equality, including when edits affect heap aliasing or virtual dispatch.
Then the challenge is to be selective about work without treating the edited method as the only place that can change?

That captures the tension at a conceptual level. An incremental analyzer seeks to avoid unnecessary full recomputation, but its result still has to reflect any consequences of the edit that matter to the reference findings, including consequences across method boundaries. The goal does not choose a particular way to identify or process those consequences.

For the incremental taint analyzer, I propose maintaining context-sensitive points-to and taint summaries, tracking the provenance of heap and dispatch dependencies, then retracting stale facts and recomputing affected SCCs after an edit.

That is a proposal for making updates selective without treating a method-body edit as purely local. The points-to summaries capture information about what references may denote, while the taint summaries capture how taint may flow. Keeping them context-sensitive is important to the proposed comparison with context-sensitive whole-program recomputation. Provenance supplies a way to relate derived facts to the heap and dispatch information they depend on; retraction and recomputation address facts that may no longer hold after an edit.
What does provenance add beyond storing the current summaries?

A current summary says what the analysis has concluded, but not necessarily why it concluded it. Provenance-tracked dependencies would record enough of that relationship to identify conclusions potentially affected when heap-aliasing or virtual-dispatch information changes. The proposal does not specify a particular provenance format or claim that simply storing dependencies is, by itself, sufficient to establish correctness.
Why maintain points-to summaries as well as taint summaries?

Points-to information can influence which heap objects a reference may access and which receiver types may reach a virtual call. Those possibilities can in turn affect taint flows. Maintaining both kinds of context-sensitive summary reflects that connection: a change in points-to information may require revisiting taint conclusions even if the edited text is not itself where a reported flow ends.
When I say heap dependencies, should that be understood as dependencies that can cross methods?

Yes, at the conceptual level of this proposal. Heap effects need not remain confined to the method where an edit occurs: a reference used in one method may relate to an object accessed through another. Provenance-tracked heap dependencies are intended to make such potential effects visible to the incremental update. No particular heap abstraction or dependency representation has been selected in the statement.
And dispatch dependencies cover changes in which implementation a virtual call may reach?

That is the relevant concern. If the possible receivers of a virtual call change, the set of implementations the analysis must consider may change as well. A taint conclusion that depends on an earlier dispatch possibility may therefore need to be reconsidered. Tracking dispatch dependencies connects that change to the summaries and facts it could affect.
I do not want an edit that removes an alias or a possible call target to leave old findings behind just because those findings were cached.

That is what retracting stale facts is meant to address. Incrementality cannot consist only of adding newly discovered facts: when an edit invalidates support for an existing fact, that fact may need to be removed and the affected analysis recomputed. The proposal identifies this need without fixing the exact rules for determining which support is stale.
Would retracting a fact automatically mean deleting every conclusion that ever depended on it?

Not necessarily as a conceptual matter. A conclusion could have more than one source of support. Provenance is relevant because it can distinguish support invalidated by an edit from support that remains. The proposal calls for retracting stale facts, not indiscriminately deleting every fact that shares a dependency with a changed one; it does not yet prescribe a specific method for handling multiple supports.
What does SCC mean here, and why recompute those?

SCC means strongly connected component: a group of nodes in a directed dependency structure that are mutually reachable. Such a component captures a cycle in which conclusions can depend on one another. Recomputing affected SCCs expresses the idea of revisiting the mutually dependent region implicated by a change, rather than assuming each affected fact can always be updated in isolation. The proposal does not specify the exact graph whose SCCs are used.
So is this a commitment to recompute the entire program whenever any cycle is touched?

No. The proposal specifically says to recompute *affected* SCCs. That expresses a selective recomputation strategy, though the proposal alone does not define the precise affectedness test or how far its consequences propagate. It should not be read either as an unconditional full-program recomputation rule or as permission to ignore dependencies beyond one component.
Can you restate how the pieces fit together after a method-body edit, without choosing a concrete implementation?

The maintained context-sensitive points-to and taint summaries provide the existing analysis information. Provenance-tracked heap and dispatch dependencies relate derived facts to information an edit might change. If that support becomes stale, the proposal calls for retracting the stale facts and recomputing the affected strongly connected components. The intent is to update interprocedural conclusions while avoiding work unrelated to the edit; the proposal does not itself establish that a particular implementation meets the correctness or speed targets.
What if the edit introduces a new alias or a new possible virtual target rather than removing one?

That still falls within the proposed dependency-aware update. New aliasing or dispatch possibilities may require additional points-to or taint conclusions, and those conclusions may affect other summaries. Retraction is especially visible when possibilities disappear, but recomputation of affected SCCs also matters when the edited program permits new possibilities. The proposal does not limit updates to deletions.
Does calling the summaries context-sensitive tell us which context representation to use?

No. It says that the maintained points-to and taint information should distinguish relevant calling contexts, consistent with the goal’s context-sensitive comparison. It does not choose a context representation, a sensitivity depth, or a summary encoding. Those would be additional design details, not facts already specified by this proposal.
Would tracking just which methods call which other methods capture the heap and dispatch dependencies I have in mind?

A caller–callee relationship alone does not express all of the conceptual dependencies named here. A heap-aliasing change can affect how taint moves through objects, and a dispatch change can alter which call relationships are possible. The proposal explicitly calls for provenance-tracked *heap and dispatch* dependencies, so reducing it to a fixed list of method-to-method links would omit what that wording is meant to cover.
Is there any claim yet that this scheme achieves the speedup target?

No measured performance or correctness result is stated. This is a proposed approach: maintain the two kinds of context-sensitive summary, track provenance for heap and dispatch dependencies, retract stale facts, and recompute affected SCCs. Whether an implementation’s findings equal sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation for Java without reflection or native calls, and whether it reaches at least a 3× median speedup over full recomputation on the fixed suite of 100 method-body edits, remain requirements rather than reported outcomes.
Which heap-alias and virtual-dispatch dependencies must invalidate context-sensitive summaries after a method-body edit?

That is the open design question. A method-body edit may change what references can alias or what implementations a virtual call can reach, and either change may affect summaries beyond the edited method. The issue is to identify which dependencies are relevant to a particular context-sensitive summary, so that a changed dependency triggers reconsideration of that summary without assuming every summary must be invalidated. The exact dependency set and invalidation rule have not been specified.
What makes a heap-alias dependency relevant to a taint summary?

Conceptually, it is relevant when the summary’s taint conclusion depends on a possible relationship between references and heap objects. For example, if a value written through one reference can be read through another because the references may alias, changing that possibility could change the taint conclusion. That example illustrates why an alias dependency may matter; it does not establish a complete rule for identifying all such dependencies.
Would it be enough to ask whether the edited method itself contains the heap read or write?

Not necessarily. The concern is interprocedural: a changed alias possibility can affect a heap access represented in another method’s context-sensitive summary. The question is therefore about dependencies of the conclusions, not just the location of the edited statement. It remains open how those dependencies should be identified and tracked.
What is the analogous dependency for virtual dispatch?

A summary may depend on which implementations a virtual call can invoke in a particular calling context. If an edit changes the possible receivers, the possible dispatch targets may change, and a conclusion based on the earlier possibilities may need to be reconsidered. The unresolved part is how precisely to represent that dependency and determine which summaries it invalidates.
Could the target of a virtual call change even when the call expression itself was not edited?

Conceptually, yes. A change in which objects may reach an existing call can change its possible targets without changing the call expression. That is why the invalidation question includes dependencies on dispatch possibilities, not solely dependencies on edited call sites.
Does 'invalidate' mean the entire summary must always be thrown away?

The question does not settle the granularity of invalidation. It asks which dependencies must cause context-sensitive summaries to be reconsidered after an edit. Depending on a design not yet specified, that could involve retracting affected facts or recomputing an affected summary or dependency region. We cannot infer from the question alone that every change requires discarding a whole summary.
How does context sensitivity complicate deciding what to invalidate?

The same method may have different analysis conclusions in different calling contexts. A heap or dispatch change might matter to some of those conclusions but not others. The question therefore asks about dependencies of *context-sensitive* summaries, rather than treating a method name alone as sufficient to identify everything affected. It does not specify the context representation or the precision attainable when distinguishing affected contexts.
Should a changed points-to conclusion be considered separately from a changed taint conclusion?

They are distinct kinds of conclusion, but they can be related: points-to information can affect heap aliasing and possible virtual targets, which can affect taint findings. For invalidation, the important conceptual question is whether a summary’s support runs through either kind of changed information. The current question does not provide a settled catalogue of dependencies or a rule for updating the two kinds of summary.
If a possible alias disappears, is that different from a new alias appearing?

Both can require reconsideration, for different intuitive reasons. Losing an alias possibility may remove support for a previously derived conclusion; gaining one may permit a conclusion that was not previously derived. In either direction, the open question is which context-sensitive summaries actually depend on that alias information and what must be revisited as a consequence.
Does the same distinction apply when a possible dispatch target disappears or appears?

Yes at that conceptual level. Removing a possible target can undermine conclusions supported through that implementation, while adding one can introduce flows that must be considered. Neither direction can be dismissed merely because the edited method’s existing taint summary appears unchanged. The precise invalidation dependencies remain to be determined.
What role does provenance play in answering this question?

Provenance is the proposed way to relate a derived fact to heap and dispatch information that supports it. In principle, such relationships could help identify which facts and summaries need reconsideration when that information changes. The open question is which relationships must be recorded to make invalidation adequate; the existence of provenance alone does not answer it.
If a fact has two independent supports and an edit affects only one, does the question require deleting the fact?

The question is about invalidating conclusions whose support may have changed, not about assuming that losing one support necessarily makes the conclusion false. Multiple supports illustrate why the dependency and retraction rules need care. No specific rule for preserving or deleting multiply supported facts is supplied here.
How far could an invalidation need to propagate?

Potentially beyond the first summary that mentions the changed alias or dispatch possibility: another summary may depend on that summary’s conclusions. The issue is whether the dependency chain can affect the final context-sensitive findings. The earlier proposal mentions recomputing affected strongly connected components, but this question does not define which components are affected or give a stopping rule for propagation.
Could I answer the question just by listing every method reachable from the edited method?

That would not, by itself, answer which *heap-alias and virtual-dispatch dependencies* must invalidate summaries. Reachability between methods is different from knowing whether a particular conclusion depends on a changed heap relationship or dispatch possibility. The question seeks the relevant dependencies; it does not yet endorse any particular reachability-based invalidation scheme.
And saying 'invalidate everything' would avoid identifying the dependencies?

It would sidestep the selectivity part of the question rather than characterize the dependencies. The broader goal includes an incremental speed target, while this question focuses on what must be reconsidered to preserve the required findings. No claim is made here that a particular broad or narrow invalidation policy meets either requirement.
Can we phrase the unresolved issue in one sentence without pretending we already have the rule?

Which changes to heap-alias relationships and possible virtual-call targets after a method-body edit can affect each context-sensitive summary, including through other summaries, and therefore require that summary’s conclusions to be revisited? That states the issue without claiming the dependency set or invalidation procedure has been established.

Here is a hypothesis for the invalidation question: tracking points-to, heap read/write, receiver-type, and call-edge provenance yields zero missed context-sensitive summary invalidations versus whole-program recomputation.

That proposes a concrete set of dependencies to track. The claim is that, after a method-body edit, those four kinds of provenance would identify every context-sensitive summary that needs invalidation when judged against whole-program recomputation. It is a hypothesis, not an established result.
Can you unpack the four kinds without turning the hypothesis into a proven rule?

Points-to provenance concerns the reference-to-object possibilities on which a conclusion depends. Heap read/write provenance concerns dependencies arising through accesses to heap state. Receiver-type provenance concerns the possible types of a virtual call’s receiver, and call-edge provenance concerns the possible calls associated with dispatch. The hypothesis is that tracking these together is sufficient to avoid *missed* context-sensitive summary invalidations; it does not say that sufficiency has been demonstrated.
Why mention both points-to and heap read/write provenance? Aren’t they the same dependency?

They describe related but different aspects of a conclusion. Points-to information concerns what a reference may denote; heap read/write information concerns accesses through references and the taint consequences those accesses may support. A change to an alias possibility matters when it changes which heap accesses can interact. Naming both makes the hypothesized coverage more explicit, without specifying how either kind of provenance is represented.
How do receiver-type and call-edge provenance differ conceptually?

Receiver-type provenance records information about the possible types reaching a virtual call. Call-edge provenance records which possible call relationships a conclusion depends on. The two can be connected, but they are not identical descriptions: a change in receiver possibilities may affect call edges, and conclusions may depend on the resulting calls. The hypothesis includes both rather than assuming that naming one automatically captures the other.
What exactly does ‘zero missed context-sensitive summary invalidations’ claim?

It claims that no context-sensitive summary requiring invalidation relative to whole-program recomputation would be overlooked. ‘Zero missed’ is about completeness of invalidation, not a count of how many summaries might be invalidated unnecessarily. The hypothesis gives no measured count and does not establish that an implementation has achieved it.
So could the hypothesis hold even if the provenance caused extra summaries to be reconsidered?

Yes. Extra invalidations would not, by themselves, constitute a *missed* invalidation. The hypothesis makes a claim about not overlooking necessary context-sensitive summary invalidations; it does not claim a minimal invalidation set or a particular amount of saved work.
Does the comparison to whole-program recomputation mean the four provenance types automatically guarantee equal taint findings?

No. Whole-program recomputation is the reference in the hypothesis for identifying missed invalidations. Avoiding missed invalidations would address one important correctness risk, but equality of final findings also depends on how affected facts are retracted and recomputed. The hypothesis should not be expanded into a demonstrated end-to-end correctness guarantee.
Suppose an edit changes which objects a reference may point to, and that changes whether a heap read can observe a write. How would this hypothesis view the dependency?

As a general illustration, the points-to relationship and the heap read/write relationship would both be candidates for provenance relevant to the affected summary. If a conclusion depends on the read observing the write, the hypothesis predicts that tracking the named provenance would prevent its required invalidation from being missed. The illustration is not evidence that the prediction is true in every case.
And if the edit changes a possible virtual target without changing the call expression?

The receiver-type and call-edge provenance are the named candidates for capturing that effect. The hypothesis predicts that a context-sensitive summary depending on the affected dispatch possibility would not escape invalidation merely because the call expression itself was unchanged. Whether the four categories actually cover every such case remains the point to assess.
Does this hypothesis pick a particular form of context sensitivity?

No. It refers to context-sensitive summaries and compares invalidation against whole-program recomputation, but it does not choose a context representation or specify how provenance is attached to contexts. Those details would matter to an implementation, yet they are not settled by the hypothesis.
Does it require recording every fact in the whole program as provenance?

It names four *kinds* of provenance to track, not a storage granularity or a requirement to record every fact in a particular way. The claim is about the resulting absence of missed summary invalidations. How much information must be retained to make that claim hold is not specified here.
Would one counterexample with a summary changed by recomputation but not invalidated under these dependencies matter?

Yes. If the comparison established that a context-sensitive summary required invalidation and the tracked dependencies failed to trigger it, that would contradict the ‘zero missed’ hypothesis. This describes what the claim means; it does not assert that such a counterexample exists.
Is the hypothesis also a claim about meeting the 3× median speedup target?

No. The hypothesis concerns invalidation coverage versus whole-program recomputation. Tracking additional provenance and reconsidering summaries have performance implications, but it states no speedup result. The separate goal remains at least a 3× median speedup over full recomputation on the fixed suite of 100 method-body edits.
Then the careful formulation is that these four dependency categories might be sufficient to avoid missed invalidations, not that they have already been shown sufficient?

Exactly. The proposed hypothesis is: tracking points-to, heap read/write, receiver-type, and call-edge provenance yields zero missed context-sensitive summary invalidations versus whole-program recomputation. It supplies a specific answer to investigate for the dependency question, while leaving its truth unverified.
To evaluate the provenance hypothesis, replay 100 AliasDispatch-100 method-body edits and compare invalidated summaries and taint findings against context-sensitive whole-program recomputation.

That sets out the evaluation activity. For each of the 100 method-body edits in AliasDispatch-100, the incremental analysis is to be compared with context-sensitive whole-program recomputation on two questions: whether it invalidates the summaries that need reconsideration, and whether its resulting taint findings match. The activity specifies a comparison, not an outcome.
Why compare invalidated summaries if we are also comparing final taint findings?

They examine different aspects of the proposed update. The invalidation comparison addresses the hypothesis that the tracked provenance yields zero missed context-sensitive summary invalidations. The findings comparison checks the resulting taint output against recomputation. Matching findings for an edit does not, by itself, show that no necessary summary invalidation was missed; conversely, identifying the right summaries to revisit does not, by itself, establish matching findings.
Whole-program recomputation does not incrementally invalidate summaries. What does it mean to compare invalidations against it?

It means using recomputation as the reference for which context-sensitive summary conclusions need reconsideration after an edit, then comparing that with what the incremental analysis invalidates. It need not mean that recomputation itself produces an incremental invalidation list. The activity does not prescribe the exact procedure for making that comparison.
Is the intended standard that the incremental analyzer invalidates exactly the same set of summaries identified through that comparison?

The stated hypothesis is about *zero missed* invalidations, not exact equality of invalidation sets. A summary reconsidered unnecessarily is different from a summary that needed reconsideration but was missed. The activity compares invalidated summaries against recomputation so that distinction can be examined; it does not declare a minimal-invalidation requirement.
What would count as a missed invalidation in this evaluation?

Conceptually, it would be a context-sensitive summary that needs reconsideration because of an edit, as indicated by the comparison with whole-program recomputation, but that the incremental analysis does not invalidate. That is the kind of discrepancy relevant to the zero-missed hypothesis. No such discrepancy, or absence of one, has been reported here.
Would an extra invalidation still be worth noting?

Yes, the comparison can distinguish extra invalidations from missed ones. An extra invalidation would not directly contradict a zero-missed claim, though it could matter to how selective the incremental work is. This activity does not report how many extra invalidations occur or assign a performance result to them.
What is the taint-findings comparison asking?

For each edited program in the replay, it asks whether the incremental analyzer’s taint findings equal those of context-sensitive whole-program recomputation. It is a comparison of the resulting findings, not just of whether the incremental analyzer ran or whether it invalidated some summaries. The node supplies no finding counts or equality results.
Could the invalidation comparison look good while the findings differ?

As a logical possibility, yes. Identifying summaries for reconsideration is only part of producing updated findings; the subsequent update also matters. That is why the activity compares both invalidated summaries and taint findings. It does not say that either comparison has already passed.
Could the findings match while the invalidation comparison exposes a problem?

It is possible for a comparison of final findings on a particular edit not to reveal every issue in an invalidation rule. The separate summary comparison is aimed at the hypothesis about missed invalidations, rather than treating matching findings on the replay as the only observation of interest. This is a reason to keep the two comparisons distinct, not a claim about the replay’s results.
Does ‘replay 100 AliasDispatch-100 method-body edits’ mean generating new edits as part of this activity?

The activity says to *replay* 100 method-body edits identified as AliasDispatch-100. It does not describe generating additional edits or changing their content. Nor does it specify individual edits, their order beyond the notion of replay, or any observed outcomes.
Why emphasize method-body edits rather than simply saying 100 program versions?

Method-body edits are the stated units of this activity and of the incremental-update setting. The question is how changes to method bodies affect context-sensitive summaries and taint findings, including effects involving heap aliasing and virtual dispatch. Calling them program versions alone would leave out that specified form of change.
Does the activity itself establish that AliasDispatch-100 covers every possible aliasing or dispatch change?

No. It names the 100 method-body edits to replay, but gives no claim that they exhaust all possible Java edits or all ways heap aliasing and virtual dispatch can change. A comparison on the named replay would be evidence about that replay; the activity alone is not a universal-coverage result.
How does this activity bear on the four provenance categories in the hypothesis?

The hypothesis names points-to, heap read/write, receiver-type, and call-edge provenance as the proposed basis for avoiding missed invalidations. Comparing the summaries invalidated after the edits with those requiring reconsideration under whole-program recomputation evaluates the prediction associated with that basis. The activity does not yet say whether the four categories suffice.
If a changed dispatch possibility affects a caller’s summary, is that within the comparison?

Yes, insofar as the caller’s context-sensitive summary needs reconsideration after one of the replayed edits, it belongs in the invalidated-summary comparison. The activity is not limited to summaries belonging to the edited method. Whether any particular edit has that effect is not specified.
And the same applies if a heap-alias change affects a summary in another method?

Yes. The comparison is about the context-sensitive summaries affected by the method-body edit, including potential interprocedural effects. A summary should not be excluded solely because it belongs to another method. The activity still leaves the actual affected summaries to be determined by the comparison, rather than listing them in advance.
Does this activity also measure the at-least-3× median speedup requirement?

This node specifies replaying 100 AliasDispatch-100 method-body edits and comparing invalidated summaries and taint findings against context-sensitive whole-program recomputation. It does not explicitly call for timing runs or report a median speedup. The broader performance goal remains separate; it should not be treated as measured by these two comparisons alone.
What should we avoid claiming before the replay and comparisons produce results?

We should not claim zero missed invalidations, equal taint findings, or a speedup on the strength of the activity description. What is specified is the evaluation: replay the 100 AliasDispatch-100 method-body edits and compare both invalidated context-sensitive summaries and taint findings with context-sensitive whole-program recomputation.

On AliasDispatch-100, all 100 of the 100 method-body edits matched the findings from context-sensitive whole-program recomputation. The invalidation also omitted zero changed context-sensitive summaries.

Those are two results for AliasDispatch-100. Across its 100 replayed method-body edits, the taint findings matched recomputation in 100/100 cases. Separately, no context-sensitive summary identified as changed was omitted from invalidation. The results concern this replay; they do not, on their own, establish what happens for every possible edit.
Are ‘100/100 findings matched’ and ‘zero changed summaries omitted’ saying the same thing?

No. The first compares the final taint findings after each edit with the findings from context-sensitive whole-program recomputation. The second concerns whether invalidation missed any context-sensitive summaries that changed. They describe different observations, even though both matter to assessing the incremental update.
Does 100/100 mean there were 100 findings?
No. The denominator counts method-body edits: findings matched recomputation for each of the 100 AliasDispatch-100 edits. The statement does not give a count of individual taint findings.
And does ‘zero changed summaries omitted’ mean no summaries changed?
No. It means the invalidation omitted none of the context-sensitive summaries identified as changed. It does not state how many summaries changed, or how many summaries were invalidated in total.
Can we infer that invalidation selected exactly the changed summaries and no others?

Not from this result. Zero omissions rules out missed changed summaries in the reported comparison, but it says nothing about whether unchanged summaries were also invalidated. Exact selection would be a stronger claim than the evidence states.
How should I describe the comparison baseline accurately?

Say that, for each of the 100 AliasDispatch-100 method-body edits, the incremental taint findings matched those from context-sensitive whole-program recomputation. For the summary comparison, say that invalidation omitted zero changed context-sensitive summaries. That keeps the findings comparison and the invalidation observation distinct.
Does this tell us that the proposed provenance categories will never miss an invalidation?

It reports zero missed changed-summary invalidations on AliasDispatch-100. It does not turn that observation into a guarantee for all Java programs or all possible method-body edits. The broader claim about tracking points-to, heap read/write, receiver-type, and call-edge provenance remains broader than this finite result.
But it is fair to say there was no missed changed summary among these 100 edits?
Yes. That is exactly the scope of the reported invalidation result: on AliasDispatch-100, invalidation omitted zero changed context-sensitive summaries across the 100 method-body edits.
Do matching findings show that every internal analysis fact was identical to recomputation?

No. The result states equality of taint findings for all 100 edits, plus the separate observation about changed context-sensitive summaries and invalidation. It does not claim that every internal fact, dependency record, or intermediate representation was identical.
Should we say that this meets the performance target?

No performance measurement is included in this evidence. It reports findings agreement and zero omitted changed summaries, not timing or a median speedup. The at-least-3× median speedup over full recomputation cannot be concluded from these results alone.
What if I want one compact sentence that retains both results and their scope?
On AliasDispatch-100, taint findings matched context-sensitive whole-program recomputation for all 100/100 method-body edits, and invalidation omitted zero changed context-sensitive summaries.
I’ve decided to select provenance-based invalidation for further development. AliasDispatch-100 showed no missed summaries, but formal soundness and speed remain unverified.

That is a decision to continue developing the approach, not a declaration that every requirement has been met. The stated reason is the absence of missed summaries on AliasDispatch-100. Formal soundness and speed are still unverified.
Does ‘select’ mean I can now describe provenance-based invalidation as sound?

No. Selecting it for further development expresses which approach to pursue. The decision explicitly leaves formal soundness unverified, so it would overstate the conclusion to call the approach formally sound on this basis.
How should I use the AliasDispatch-100 result when explaining the decision?

You can say that AliasDispatch-100 showed no missed summaries and that this motivated selecting provenance-based invalidation for further development. Keep the observation tied to AliasDispatch-100; the decision does not turn it into a claim about all possible method-body edits.
Is ‘no missed summaries’ a statement about speed?
No. It concerns invalidation coverage in the named replay. It gives no timing result, and the decision expressly says speed remains unverified.
Could I say that avoiding missed summaries proves the whole incremental analyzer correct?

That would go beyond this decision. Avoiding missed summaries in AliasDispatch-100 is the stated reason for selecting the invalidation approach. Formal soundness of the analyzer remains unverified; the decision does not equate the observed invalidation result with a proof of end-to-end correctness.
What does ‘for further development’ add?

It limits the commitment. Provenance-based invalidation is the selected direction to develop further, while the stated uncertainties remain open. It does not say that development is complete or that formal soundness or speed has been established.
Does the decision specify a new way to represent provenance?

Can we describe the suite targets as met without saying the general analyzer goal is proved?

Yes. The decision explicitly makes that distinction. The 100/100 finding agreement and 3.6× median speedup meet the AliasDispatch-100 suite targets, while formal soundness remains unproven. Empirical agreement across the suite is not a proof that the analyzer matches the sound whole-program result for every Java program in scope.
What is the scope of the broader soundness requirement?

For Java without reflection or native calls, the analyzer’s findings must equal those from sound, context-sensitive whole-program recomputation, including when method-body edits change heap aliasing or virtual dispatch. The release-candidate decision does not claim that this general requirement has been formally proved.
Does ‘unproven’ mean the suite found a soundness failure?
No. Formal soundness remaining unproven is a statement about the absence of a formal proof here, not a report of a failure. The stated suite result is finding parity on all 100 edits.
Would it be accurate to write that v0.4 is formally sound because it passed every suite edit?

No. Passing all 100 edits establishes the reported finding parity on that suite. It does not by itself establish formal soundness across the stated Java scope, and the decision expressly says formal soundness remains unproven.
Does the measured median speedup establish that every edit is at least three times faster than recomputation?
No. A 3.6× median does not give individual speedups. The suite-level median meets the ≥3× target, but the decision makes no per-edit runtime claim.
Should the 3.6× number be described as a reduction in facts revisited?

No. It is a measured median runtime speedup relative to full recomputation on the sequential AliasDispatch-100 replay. A fact-revisit fraction is a different measurement and is not the basis of this release-candidate decision.
Does this decision certify identical internal points-to and call-graph facts?

It does not. The reported parity concerns taint findings, while the formal fixpoint-equivalence question remains open. Describing every internal analysis fact as identical to recomputation would add a conclusion not stated in the decision.
Can we say the release candidate has met its empirical suite goals even though a proof is outstanding?

Yes. That is the decision’s balance: select v0.4 as release candidate because the 100/100 finding-parity and 3.6× median-speedup results meet the suite targets, while explicitly retaining the qualification that formal soundness remains unproven.
